source_text: τὰ δ’ ἑξῆς προςαποδοτέον καὶ τὴν ἐκ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας Ελληνικὴν κλοπὴν σαφέστερον ἤδη παραστατέον. Φασὶ γὰρ σῶμα εἶναι τὸν θεὸν οἱ Στωϊκοὶ καὶ πνεῦμα κατ’ οὐσίαν, ὥσπερ ἀμέλει καὶ τὴν ψυχήν. πάντα ταῦτα ἄντικρυς εὑρήσεις ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς. μὴ γάρ μοι τὰς ἀλληγορίας αὐτῶν ἐννοήσῃς τὰ νῦν ὡς ἡ γνωστικὴ παραδίδωσιν ἀλήθεια, εἰ ἄλλο τι δεικνύουσαι, καθάπερ οἱ σοφοὶ παλαισταί, ἄλλο μηνύουσιν. ἀλλ’ οἳ μὲν διήκειν διὰ πάσης τῆς οὐσίας τὸν θεόν φασιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ ποιητὴν μόνον αὐτὸν καλοῦμεν καὶ λόγῳ ποιητήν. παρήγαγεν δὲ αὐτοὺς τὸ ἐν τῇ Σοφίᾳ εἰρημένον διήκει δὲ καὶ χωρεῖ διὰ πάντων διὰ τὴν καθαριότητα, ἐπεὶ μὴ συνῆκαν λέγεσθαι ταῦτα ἐπὶ τῆς σοφίας τῆς πρωτοκτίστου τῷ θεῷ. ναί, φασίν, ἀλλὰ ὕλην ὑποτίθενται οἱ φιλόσοφοι ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς, οἵ τε Στωϊκοὶ καὶ Πλάτων καὶ Πυθαγόρας, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης ὁ Περιπατητικός, οὐχὶ δὲ μίαν ἀρχήν. ἴστωσαν οὖν τὴν καλουμένην ὕλην ἄποιον καὶ ἀσχημάτιστον λεγομένην πρὸς αὐτῶν, καὶ τολμηρότερον ἤδη μὴ ὂν πρὸς τοῦ Πλάτωνος εἰρῆσθαι. καὶ μή τι μυστικώτατα μίαν τὴν ὄντως οὖσαν ἀρχὴν εἰδὼς ἐν τῷ Τιμαίῳ αὐταῖς φησι λέξεσιν· νῦν δ’ οὖν τὸ παρ’ ἡμῶν ὧδε ἐχέτω· τὴν μὲν περὶ πάντων εἴτε ἀρχὴν εἴτε ἀρχὰς εἴτε ὅπῃ δοκεῖ τούτων πέρι, τὸ νῦν οὐ ῥητέον, δἰ ἄλλο μὲν οὐδέν, διὰ δὲ τὸ χαλεπὸν εἶναι κατὰ τὸν παρόντα τρόπον τῆς διεξόδου δηλῶσαι τὰ δοκοῦντα. ἄλλως τε ἡ λέξις ἡ προφητικὴ ἐκείνη ἡ δὲ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος ἀφορμὰς αὐτοῖς ὑλικῆς οὐσίας παρέσχηται. Ναὶ μὴν Ἐπικούρῳ μὲν ἡ τοῦ αὐτομάτου παρείσδυσις οὐ παρακολουθήσαντι τῷ ῥητῷ γέγονεν ἐντεῦθεν ματαιότης ματαιοτήτων, τὰ πάντα ματαιότης. Ἀριστοτέλει δὲ μέχρι σελήνης ἐπῆλθε καταγαγεῖν τὴν πρόνοιαν ἐκ τοῦδε τοῦ ψαλμοῦ· κύριε, ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν. οὐδέπω γὰρ ἀποκεκάλυπτο ἡ τῶν προφητικῶν δήλωσις μυστηρίων πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κυρίου παρουσίας. Τάς τε αὖ μετὰ θάνατον κολάσεις καὶ τὴν διὰ πυρὸς τιμωρίαν ἀπὸ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας ἥ τε ποιητικὴ πᾶσα μοῦσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ φιλοσοφία ὑφείλετο. Πλάτων γοῦν ἐν τῷ τελευταίῳ τῆς Πολιτείας αὐταῖς φησι ταῖς λέξεσιν· ἐνταῦθα δὴ ἄνδρες ἄγριοι, διάπυροι ἰδεῖν, παρεστῶτες, καταμανθάνοντες τὸ φθέγμα, τοὺς μὲν ἰδίᾳ παραλαβόντες ἦγον, τὸν δὲ Ἀριδαῖον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους συμποδίσαντες χεῖράς τε καὶ πόδας καὶ κεφαλήν, καταβαλόντες καὶ ἐκδείραντες, εἷλκον παρὰ τὴν ὁδὸν ἐκτὸς ἐπ’ ἀσπαλάθων κνάπτοντες. οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἄνδρες οἱ διάπυροι ἀγγέλους αὐτῷ βούλονται δηλοῦν, οἳ παραλαβόντες τοὺς ἀδίκους κολάζουσιν· ὁ ποιῶν, φησί, τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πῦρ φλέγον. ἕπεται δὲ τούτοις τὴν ψυχὴν εἶναι ἀθάνατον. τὸ γὰρ κολαζόμενον ἢ παιδευόμενον ἐν αἰσθήσει ὂν ζῇ, κἂν πάσχειν λέγηται. τί δ’; οὐκ οἶδεν ὁ Πλάτων καὶ πυρὸς ποταμοὺς καὶ τῆς γῆς τὸ βάθος, τὴν πρὸς τῶν βαρβάρων Γέενναν καλουμένην Τάρταρον ποιητικῶς ὀνομάζων, Κωκυτόν τε καὶ Ἀχέροντα καὶ Πυριφλεγέθοντα καὶ τοιαῦτά τινα εἰς τὴν παίδευσιν σωφρονίζοντα παρεισάγων κολαστήρια; τῶν μικρῶν δὲ κατὰ τὴν γραφὴν καὶ ἐλαχίστων τοὺς ἀγγέλους τοὺς ὁρῶντας τὸν θεόν, πρὸς δὲ καὶ τὴν εἰς ἡμᾶς δἰ ἀγγέλων τῶν ἐφεστώτων ἥκουσαν ἐπισκοπὴν ἐμφαίνων οὐκ ὀκνεῖ γράφειν·
pass_a_gloss: But the next things must be returned and the Greek theft from barbarian philosophy must now be shown more clearly. For the Stoics say that God is a body and spirit in essence, just as also the soul. You will find all these things stated plainly in the scriptures. Do not think that I am considering their allegories now as the gnosis delivers the truth, if they show something else, just like the wrestlers, they indicate something else. But they say that God passes through all of existence, we however call him only the creator and the creator by word. The statement in Wisdom led them astray, 'he passes through and fills all things because of his purity,' since they did not understand that these things were being said about the primal wisdom of God. Yes, they say, but the philosophers hypothesize matter in the beginnings, both the Stoics and Plato and Pythagoras, and also Aristotle the Peripatetic, not one principle. Let them know that the so-called matter is void and unqualified, as it is said, and it is even more daring to say this against Plato. And in the Timaeus, he says in these very words, knowing the one truly existing principle in a most mystical way. Now therefore let our position be as follows: the thing about all things, whether it is a principle or principles or however it seems, is not to be spoken now, because of nothing else, but because it is difficult to show the things that seem in the present manner of exposition. Besides, the prophetic speech, 'the earth was invisible and unformed,' has provided them with a basis for material existence. Indeed, Epicurus did not follow the statement, and from this, emptiness of emptinesses has come, all things are emptiness. Aristotle drew down providence to the moon from this psalm, 'Lord, your mercy and your truth reach to the clouds.' For the explanation of prophetic mysteries had not yet been revealed before the coming of the Lord. The punishments after death and the punishment by fire, and all the poetic Muses, but also Greek philosophy, have been borrowed from barbarian philosophy. Plato, in the last book of the Republic, says in these very words: 'Here indeed, fierce men, fiery to see, standing, learning the voice, having taken some privately, led them away, but having bound the hands and feet and head of Aridaeus and the others, having thrown them down and flayed them, they dragged them along the road outside, striking them with asphalathoi.' For the men, the fiery ones, want to indicate angels, who, having taken the unjust, punish them; he says, 'the one who makes his angels spirits and his servants a burning fire.' It follows that the soul is immortal. For what is punished or educated, being in sensation, lives, even if it is said to suffer. What? Does Plato not know of rivers of fire and the depth of the earth, calling the Gehenna of the barbarians Tartarus in a poetic way, introducing fiery punishments for education, such as Cocytus and Acheron and Pyriphlegethon, and other such things? As for the small and least things, according to scripture, the angels who see God, and also the oversight that has come to us through the angels who stand over us, he does not hesitate to write.

pass_b_english: We must now return to the remaining points and demonstrate more clearly the Greek theft from barbarian philosophy. The Stoics claim that God is a body and spirit in essence, just as they also claim the soul is. You will find all these things stated plainly in the scriptures. Do not suppose that I am now treating their allegories as the gnostic tradition hands down the truth, for if they demonstrate one thing while signaling another, they are like wrestlers who feint one way and throw another. The Stoics say that God pervades all existence, but we call him only the Creator, the Maker by his Word. The passage in Wisdom led them astray: ‘For she passes through and penetrates all things because of her purity’ (Wisdom 7:24), since they failed to understand that these words refer to the primordial Wisdom created by God. ‘Yes,’ they say, ‘but the philosophers posit matter as a first principle—the Stoics, Plato, Pythagoras, and Aristotle the Peripatetic as well—not a single principle.’ Let them acknowledge that this so-called matter is described by them as void and unqualified, and it is even more boldly said by Plato that it is non-being. And in the Timaeus, knowing the one truly existing principle in a most mystical way, he speaks in these very words. Now, then, let our position be this: the question concerning all things, whether it is a principle or principles or whatever one thinks about them, is not to be discussed now, for no other reason than that it is difficult to set forth the apparent truths in the present mode of exposition. Besides, the prophetic word, ‘The earth was invisible and unformed’ (Gen 1:2), has supplied them with a starting-point for material substance. Indeed, Epicurus, because he did not attend to the oracle, fell from this into vanity of vanities: ‘All is vanity.’ Aristotle, drawing providence down only as far as the moon from this psalm, ‘Lord, your mercy is in the heavens, and your truth reaches to the clouds’ (Ps 36:5), limited it thus because the prophetic revelation of mysteries had not yet been disclosed before the Lord’s coming. The punishments after death and the punishment by fire were borrowed from barbarian philosophy by the entire poetic Muse, and by Greek philosophy as well. In the last book of the Republic, Plato writes in these very words: ‘Here, indeed, wild men, fiery to look upon, stood by, discerning the voice; taking some privately, they led them away, but binding the hands and feet and head of Aridaeus and the others, throwing them down and flaying them, they dragged them along the road outside, tearing them on thorns.’ The fiery men, he says, represent angels who, seizing the unjust, punish them; ‘He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire’ (Ps 104:4). It follows from this that the soul is immortal. For whatever is punished or disciplined while endowed with sensation lives on, even if it is said to suffer. What? Does Plato not know of rivers of fire and the depths of the earth, poetically naming the barbarians’ Gehenna ‘Tartarus,’ and introducing Cocytus, Acheron, Pyriphlegethon, and such like as correctional punishments for discipline? And regarding the ‘little ones’ of scripture, he does not hesitate to write of the angels who behold God, and of the oversight that has come to us through the angels set over us.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, while Pass B provides a more fluent version with necessary scripture citations (Wisdom 7:24, Gen 1:2, Ps 36:5, Ps 104:4) which are required for clarity in patristic contexts. The translation of 'ἀσπαλάθων' as 'asphalathoi' (Pass A) and 'thorns' (Pass B) is acceptable as the Greek term refers to a specific type of thorny/rough ground. The distinction between the Stoic view and the author's view of the Creator is preserved.
